idiom_name: cockatiel circuitBreaker(handleX, {...}) + wrap(...) with typed policies
implementation_notes: TypeScript's advantage is that the breaker and its classification are typed: cockatiel's IPolicy<Context> contract (execute<T>(fn, signal) plus onSuccess/onFailure events) composes breakers with retry, timeout and bulkhead through wrap(...), the trip rule is a breaker strategy object (ConsecutiveBreaker, CountBreaker, SamplingBreaker), and handleType(NetworkError).orWhen(...) or handleWhenResult(res => res.status >= 500) makes failure classification part of the type-checked code rather than an untyped option. Use it for browser and Node targets alike. When the project is Node-only and prefers an EventEmitter-style breaker with percentile statistics, opossum with @types/opossum is the alternative, and the same decisions apply: one breaker per dependency, a bounded call duration, and explicit classification of business errors.
pitfalls: Types do not enforce state: a policy created inside a request handler compiles fine and resets the breaker on every call, so declare policies as module-level constants.
handleAll treats every rejection as a failure, so business errors typed as Error subclasses still trip the breaker unless handleType or handleWhen narrows it.
The AbortSignal in the execution context must be forwarded to fetch or the HTTP client, or the breaker's timeout rejects the promise while the request keeps running in the background.
In multi-instance deployments the breaker is per process, so all replicas trip independently unless the state is externalised.
